title: What antenatal care is
answer: Antenatal care (ANC) is the regular health check-ups you get from a nurse, midwife or doctor while you are pregnant. At these visits the health worker checks your health and the baby's growth, offers tests, gives vaccines and supplements, and answers your questions. ANC also helps you plan where and how you will give birth. In Rwanda you can get antenatal care at your nearest health center. It is for every pregnant person, whatever your age or situation.

title: Why antenatal care matters
answer: Antenatal care helps you and your baby stay healthy. Health workers can find problems early, like high blood pressure, anaemia, infections or a baby that is not growing well, and treat them before they become dangerous. You get vaccines, supplements and advice on food, rest and danger signs. Mothers who attend antenatal care regularly are more likely to have a safe birth and a healthy baby. Even if you feel fine, the check-ups are still important.

title: When to start antenatal care
answer: Start antenatal care as early as possible, ideally in the first 12 weeks (first three months) of pregnancy. Go as soon as you think you are pregnant or have a positive test. Starting early lets the health worker confirm how far along you are, check your health, offer important tests and give supplements that help the baby's early development. If you are already further along, it is never too late. Go to your nearest health center now.

title: How many antenatal care contacts are recommended
answer: WHO recommends at least eight antenatal care contacts during pregnancy. The first should be in the first 12 weeks, then around 20 and 26 weeks, then more often near the end of pregnancy, at about 30, 34, 36, 38 and 40 weeks. Your health center may use its own schedule, so ask them when to come back. If you have a health problem, you may need extra visits. Write down each appointment date so you do not miss it.

title: What happens at the first antenatal visit
answer: At your first antenatal visit, the health worker will ask about your health, your last period and any past pregnancies. They will check your weight, height and blood pressure and may examine your belly. You will be offered blood and urine tests, including tests for HIV, syphilis and anaemia. You may get a tetanus vaccine and iron and folic acid. They will estimate your due date and explain danger signs. It is a good time to ask any question.

title: What happens at later antenatal visits
answer: At later antenatal visits, the health worker checks your blood pressure and weight, measures your belly to see if the baby is growing well, and listens to the baby's heartbeat. Near the end of pregnancy they check the baby's position. They may repeat some tests, continue your supplements and ask how you feel. They also help you make a birth plan and remind you of danger signs. Tell them about any pain, bleeding or worries.

title: Blood tests during antenatal care
answer: During antenatal care you will be offered blood tests that protect you and your baby. These usually check your blood level for anaemia, your blood group, and infections like HIV, syphilis and sometimes hepatitis B. Some infections can pass to the baby, but if they are found early, treatment can protect the baby. The tests are confidential, and the health worker should explain each one and the results to you. You can ask questions before agreeing.

title: Urine test in pregnancy
answer: At antenatal visits you may be asked for a small urine sample. Health workers use it to look for protein, which can be a sign of a serious blood pressure problem called pre-eclampsia, and for sugar or signs of a urine infection. Urine infections in pregnancy can be harmless to treat but risky if ignored. Giving a sample is simple and painless. If you have pain or burning when you pass urine, tell the nurse.

title: Blood pressure checks in pregnancy
answer: Your blood pressure is checked at every antenatal visit because high blood pressure in pregnancy can be dangerous for you and your baby. It often has no signs at first, so the check is the only way to catch it early. The test is quick: a cuff is put on your arm and squeezes for a moment. If your blood pressure is high, the health worker will explain what to do and may ask you to come back more often.

title: Tetanus vaccine in pregnancy
answer: Tetanus is a serious infection that can kill newborn babies, often through an unclean umbilical cord or an unsafe birth. A tetanus vaccine given during pregnancy protects both you and your baby. It is safe in pregnancy. How many injections you need depends on how many you have had before, so bring any vaccination card you have. Your health worker at antenatal care will tell you when to get each dose.

title: Iron and folic acid supplements in pregnancy
answer: Pregnant women are usually given iron and folic acid tablets at antenatal care. Iron helps prevent anaemia (weak blood), which can make you tired and make birth riskier. Folic acid helps the baby's brain and spine develop well. Take them exactly as your health worker explains and do not share them. They can sometimes cause stomach upset or dark stools; if this bothers you, tell the nurse rather than stopping on your own.

title: Anaemia in pregnancy
answer: Anaemia means your blood does not have enough healthy red cells to carry oxygen. It is common in pregnancy. Signs can include feeling very tired, weak, dizzy, short of breath, or having pale eyelids, palms or lips. Anaemia can make bleeding at birth more dangerous and affect the baby's growth. Health workers test for it at antenatal care. Eating iron-rich foods, taking supplements as advised and preventing malaria all help. If you notice these signs, see a health worker.

title: Sleeping under a mosquito net in pregnancy
answer: Malaria is more dangerous during pregnancy, so the best daily protection is to sleep under an insecticide-treated mosquito net every night, all year. Tuck the net in well and repair any holes. Also keep the area around your home free of standing water and close doors and windows in the evening. In Rwanda, pregnant women can often receive a treated net through antenatal care, so ask at your health center if you do not have one.

title: Why malaria is dangerous in pregnancy
answer: Malaria can be more severe during pregnancy. It can cause serious anaemia in the mother, and can lead to miscarriage, early birth, a small baby or stillbirth. Signs include fever, chills, headache and body pain. If you are pregnant and have a fever, go to the health center the same day to be tested; do not wait or treat yourself at home. Malaria in pregnancy needs medicine chosen by a health worker that is safe for the baby.

title: Deworming during pregnancy
answer: Intestinal worms can take nutrients from your body and add to anaemia. In places where worms are common, health workers may give a deworming medicine to pregnant women after the first three months of pregnancy, when it is considered safe. Do not take deworming medicine on your own in early pregnancy; ask at antenatal care. You can also prevent worms by washing hands with soap, wearing shoes, drinking safe water and washing fruit and vegetables.

title: Partner attending antenatal care
answer: Your partner is welcome and encouraged to come with you to antenatal care, especially the first visit. In Rwanda, couples are encouraged to attend together. If your partner cannot or will not come, you can still get full care on your own. Your care does not depend on bringing anyone.

title: Health insurance for pregnancy care
answer: In Rwanda, community-based health insurance (mutuelle de santé) helps cover care at public health centers and hospitals, including antenatal care, giving birth and postnatal care. Make sure your mutuelle is paid and up to date before your due date, and carry your card. If you are unsure whether you are covered or cannot afford it, talk to your community health worker, the health center or local leaders, or call 114 for information.

title: Weight gain in pregnancy
answer: Gaining weight during pregnancy is normal and healthy. It comes from the growing baby, placenta, extra blood, fluid and some stored fat for breastfeeding. Most weight is gained in the second half of pregnancy. How much is right depends on your weight before pregnancy, so the health worker weighs you at each visit. Gaining too little or too much can both be a concern. Do not try to diet or lose weight while pregnant; ask your health worker for advice.

title: Taking medicines while pregnant
answer: Some medicines can harm a baby, especially in the first months of pregnancy. Do not stop medicine for a long-term illness without advice either, as that can also be risky. When you are sick, the best place to get safe treatment is the health center.

title: Traditional herbs during pregnancy
answer: Some people use traditional herbs or remedies during pregnancy, for example to make labour faster. title: Healthy eating in pregnancy
answer: A healthy pregnancy diet includes a variety of foods every day: staples like sweet potatoes, cassava, maize or rice; beans, peas, groundnuts, eggs, fish or meat for protein; dark green vegetables like dodo (amaranth) and cassava leaves; fruits; and milk if you can. Eat an extra small meal or snack each day. Use iodised salt, limit sugary drinks and very salty food, and drink clean water. Good food helps your baby grow and keeps you strong.

title: The eating for two myth
answer: You do not need to eat twice as much when pregnant. Your body needs only a little more food, roughly one extra small meal or healthy snack a day, especially in the second half of pregnancy. What matters more is eating a variety of nutritious foods. Eating far too much can lead to unhealthy weight gain, while eating too little can harm the baby's growth. Listen to your hunger and ask your health worker if you are unsure.

title: Iron-rich foods in pregnancy
answer: Iron helps your body make blood for you and your baby. Good sources of iron include beans, peas, lentils, dark green leafy vegetables like amaranth (dodo) and cassava leaves, eggs, liver, meat, fish and small dried fish (indagara). Eating fruits with vitamin C, like oranges, passion fruit or tomatoes, at the same meal helps your body absorb iron. Tea or coffee with meals can reduce iron absorption, so have them between meals instead.

title: Food safety in pregnancy
answer: During pregnancy your body is more sensitive to some food infections, which can harm the baby. Wash hands before cooking and eating, wash fruit and vegetables with clean water, cook meat, fish and eggs well until no pink or runny parts remain, and drink boiled or pasteurised milk. Avoid food left uncovered for a long time and drink safe water. These simple steps help prevent food poisoning and infections.

title: Iodised salt in pregnancy
answer: Iodine is important for the baby's brain development. A lack of iodine in pregnancy can harm the baby's growth and learning. The easiest way to get enough iodine is to use iodised salt in your cooking instead of non-iodised salt. You only need normal amounts; do not add a lot of extra salt. Store salt in a covered container away from heat and sunlight so it keeps its iodine.

title: Vegetarian diet in pregnancy
answer: If you do not eat meat or fish, you can still have a healthy pregnancy. Eat plenty of beans, peas, lentils, soybeans, groundnuts and other nuts for protein and iron. If you eat eggs and milk, they are excellent. Add dark green vegetables and fruits rich in vitamin C to help absorb iron. Take your iron and folic acid supplements as advised. Tell your health worker about your diet so they can check you have enough nutrients.

title: Milk and calcium in pregnancy
answer: Calcium helps build your baby's bones and teeth and helps protect you, including against some blood pressure problems. Good sources include milk, yoghurt (ikivuguto), small fish eaten with their bones like indagara, dark green leafy vegetables and beans. Drink milk that is boiled or pasteurised. If you cannot get milk, eat the other calcium foods. Your health worker may also advise a calcium supplement.
